judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a member declared by a generated partial source
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the same correct, minimal refactor and satisfy both rubric requirements. B provides stronger evidence of behavior preservation: it establishes a green baseline, verifies the template generation setup, builds after the edit, and runs the full tests successfully on both net8.0 and net10.0 (17 tests each). A builds successfully but does not run tests or inspect the generation source relationship.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a method without breaking a configured reflection name
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agents produced the same required refactor, preserved reflection compatibility through an appropriate private shim, left the old-name compatibility exercise intact, and successfully built and tested Fixture.sln. Differences are only wording of the XML documentation and final summary, not result quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a shipped public method without breaking existing callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The two final results are materially equivalent and fully satisfy all three requirements: both preserve the shipped API through an obsolete forwarding shim, migrate ordinary callers while retaining an executed legacy test, update the unshipped API manifest, and validate clean successful builds/tests across both TFMs.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename an internal member used by a friend assembly
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs produce the same complete two-file rename, preserve behavior, migrate the sole friend-assembly caller, and successfully validate the solution (17 passing tests for net8.0 and net10.0). Run 2's explicit post-change build is somewhat more documented, but does not create a material final-result advantage because Run 1's solution test also compiles the solution successfully.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename one binding without touching same-text symbols
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final results fully satisfy the requested refactor and preservation requirements. Response B additionally runs an explicit build before testing, whereas Response A's dotnet test invocation also builds the solution and provides equivalent successful compilation and test evidence; this does not create a material final-result quality difference.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for an ordinary feature request
judgeRationales.rationale: The final code changes are functionally equivalent and fully satisfy the requested tier and pricing-flow integration. Both agents also validated the result with passing test suites; neither has a meaningful quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a new hook when an optional predecessor is absent
judgeRationales.rationale: Although both diagnose the condition correctly, B is the only response that gives a fully compliant fix: optional remains conditional and ordered first, while required is unconditional and therefore cannot be silently skipped. A's primary generic solution masks a missing required file, violating a central requirement.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Repair stale generation after input membership changes
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides a direct, targeted and generally sound manifest-as-input repair with a useful verification plan. A's conceptual diagnosis is good, but its offered repair is technically unreliable and its claimed unchanged-build behavior conflicts with its own manifest serialization, so it fails the central requirement not to turn the catalog work into an every-build rebuild. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Review framework conditions without breaking valid F sharp items
judgeRationales.rationale: The final answers are effectively equivalent in content and quality. Both get the property-timing diagnosis and F# ordering right, but share the same important error of treating the PackageReference ItemGroup as having the identical early-condition defect and unnecessarily moving it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Separate dependency waits from expensive compilation
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give sound core advice: summed reference-resolution waits are not a reason to remove dependency edges or disable parallelism, and the dependency compile warrants investigation. B is stronger because it explicitly seeks analyzer/generator attribution, gives more nuanced reference-edge guidance, and calls for controlled repeated comparisons. Its omission of explicit output-preservation validation prevents a larger advantage.

judgeRationales.rationale: B fully follows the governing refactoring constraint: it correctly declines a feature request, preserves behavior, confirms no changes, and routes it appropriately. A performs precisely the prohibited behavioral feature work, so it fails every rubric criterion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Capture a failing invocation without repairing it
judgeRationales.rationale: Both successfully delivered a verified binary log and the correct original nonzero exit code. B is the better response because it more faithfully honored the capture-only/no-investigation constraint and used a fresh, explicitly verified artifact name. The gap is limited because A still captured the required log correctly and made no repairs or destructive changes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose a failed build from its only surviving artifact
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide a correct, well-supported diagnosis and minimal non-destructive repair. B is modestly stronger because it unambiguously separates binlog replay from rebuilding and explicitly states no repair or rebuild was performed given the missing checkout.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep an npm failure outside MSBuild
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are accurate, concise answers to a TypeScript/Vite TS2307 alias-resolution failure and appropriately avoid .NET guidance. B is marginally stronger because it retains the essential first checks while covering common build-specific failure modes such as case sensitivity and the active tsconfig configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep failing assertions out of build troubleshooting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are solid, responsive debugging plans that honor the constraints. B is marginally more complete and targeted for a one-cent discrepancy by identifying explicit midpoint policy and rounding-order mismatches, while still clearly ruling out a build problem.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep framework migration separate from build cleanup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly avoid editing files and acknowledge the missing app, but B still delivers a useful, appropriately scoped general migration plan with substantive compatibility risks and testing. A stops after requesting more information, leaving the user without the requested plan.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep legacy project conversion with the migration workflow
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep runtime CPU profiling out of build diagnosis
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are good, responsive runtime-investigation answers that comply with the central constraint. B is modestly better due to its clearer boundary from build diagnostics, more explicit no-install/no-change framing, and somewhat more actionable explanation of the collected evidence.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Leave a valid packed import contract unchanged
judgeRationales.rationale: B reaches the correct package-layout-based answer and addresses every key rationale: configured nuspec resolution, packed contract, the danger of a guard, and no reorganization. A bases its conclusion on the irrelevant raw source-tree absence and recommends the exact change that would mask a future broken package.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a new hook when an optional predecessor is absent
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers diagnose the core MSBuild behavior and offer workable ordered decompositions. B is clearer about semicolon-list import semantics and, importantly, identifies the mandatory required import must be unguarded to fail explicitly. Its main sample still guards required.targets, so the edge is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject an unsupported build speedup claim
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct, clear, and satisfy the central caution against the unsupported 2x claim. B is overall stronger because its compact plan explicitly separates full, changed-input, and no-op measurements and adds binlog evidence; A is somewhat stronger on alternating more repetitions but omits the changed-input case.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Repair stale generation after input membership changes
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Review framework conditions without breaking valid F sharp items
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the precisely scoped required change: relocate only the early conditioned property group. A gets the property and compile-order portions right, but makes a central MSBuild evaluation-order error by treating the PackageReference item condition as broken and prescribing an unnecessary relocation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Separate dependency waits from expensive compilation
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are substantively strong on the core timing interpretation and correctly reject the two unsupported remedies, while both share the important omission of an equivalent-build/output-preservation validation plan. B is marginally better overall because its dependency-graph caveat makes the advice against altering references more precise without weakening the conclusion.

judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly implements the requested repository-level .NET configuration: global.json gets both local SDK discovery and actionable native missing-SDK guidance while preserving prior sections. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect incompatible .NET host version

A gives the opposite conclusion, makes a fundamental factual error about feature availability, and instructs the user to perform a setup that cannot work with the stated host SDK.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Plan a project-local .NET 11 preview setup without downloading
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested setup element, most importantly the local-first `$host$` fallback resolution, gitignore entry, and cleanup instructions. A offers a workable local install outline but misses three explicit rubric requirements and its environment configuration conflicts with the requested fallback behavior.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Extract subtotal calculation without changing arithmetic
judgeRationales.rationale: Both Response A and Response B executed the refactoring task with identical technical outcomes. The final code in OrderProcessor.cs is byte-for-byte identical in both cases: the subtotal loop was extracted into a private static CalculateSubtotal method without any changes to the logic, and the method is correctly called from DoStuff. Both solutions preserved decimal arithmetic (all decimal literals and operations unchanged), maintained the original evaluation order, and produced invoice results that passed all 17 tests on both .NET 8.0 and 10.0. While Run B used a refactoring skill and completed slightly faster, and Run A used a traditional methodical approach, these operational differences do not affect the quality or correctness of the final output, which is the primary evaluation criterion. Both are equally successful refactorings."

Response B took a mechanical approach that required two patches - first creating then fixing a redundant assertion. While both achieved the same final state with passing tests, Response A better fulfilled the rubric's requirement for 'one focused operation' and showed better code quality judgment." judgeRationales.rationale: The two final code results are effectively identical: each achieves single-source parsing and preserves both ConfigReader methods, but each reverses the specified delegation direction. Neither run has a quality advantage over the other.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline a framework and package upgrade dressed up as a refactor
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every explicit rubric requirement with a clear refusal and correct routing. A directly violates all three by modifying the project and falsely characterizing version upgrades as a behavior-preserving refactor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline a new-feature request dressed up as a refactor
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Extract shared discount logic without collapsing distinct inputs
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agents delivered the same correct refactor in the final code, explicitly preserved the separate invoice and quote bases, and successfully verified Fixture.sln with builds and all 17 tests passing across both target frameworks.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Extract subtotal calculation without changing arithmetic
judgeRationales.rationale: The resulting refactor is substantively identical in both runs: a direct call to a private helper containing the original loop, with invoice behavior validated by successful multi-target builds and tests. The static versus instance helper choice has no relevant quality or behavioral impact here.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Inline a pass-through wrapper and update callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The final code changes are substantively identical and satisfy both requested refactoring requirements. Both runs also recover from an initially unsuccessful validation command and ultimately show passing net8.0 and net10.0 tests; neither has a final-result quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep a shipped nullable contract out of a refactor
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs make the prohibited source-contract change and mischaracterize it as behavior-preserving. A is only slightly preferable because it does not additionally rewrite the shipped API record; B compounds the same core mistake by formally recording the breaking contract change. B's stronger build/test evidence does not overcome the rubric's requirement to leave the API unchanged.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep behavior-changing bug fixes out of a behavior-preserving refactor
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly resolves the contradiction in the request: it performs and validates the rename while preserving the $100 invoice behavior and clearly deferring the non-refactor. A performs a real invoice-behavior change, modifies tests to mask the changed expectation, and mislabels the combined work as a refactor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Merge two near-identical types into one parameterized type
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a serialized name while renaming a C# property
judgeRationales.rationale: The final code changes are substantively equivalent and fully meet both requirements: Tier is the C# API, callers are migrated, and explicit serialization metadata plus a serialization test preserve LoyaltyLevel on the wire. Minor presentation/source-layout differences do not affect correctness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve a shipped wrapper while inlining ordinary callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The two agents produced the same substantive code change and equivalent validation: ordinary callers use CurrencyFormatter.Format, the legacy public forwarder remains, and Fixture.sln builds/tests pass. Their shared potential omission of an explicit Obsolete attribute affects both equally.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a helper used in every target-framework branch
judgeRationales.rationale: The actual edits and successful multi-target tests are equivalent. B's final report is more accurate and evidence-aligned: it correctly reports 17 passing tests on each framework and names the exact preserved output strings, whereas A has a clear typo claiming net10 passed "17/10" despite its own evidence showing 17/17.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a member declared by a generated partial source
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses completed the requested behavior-preserving rename in exactly the two required source files and reported successful build/test validation. There is no material difference in final-result correctness or quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a method without breaking a configured reflection name
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly implements the requested compatibility design and validates the multi-target solution. A produces passing tests but substitutes a custom attribute-based reflection resolution mechanism for the expressly required private old-name forwarding shim, adding unnecessary behavior and weakening general reflection-name compatibility. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename a shipped public method without breaking existing callers
judgeRationales.rationale: The final results are materially the same and satisfy all three requested behaviors: renamed primary API and ordinary callers, obsolete forwarding compatibility member, preserved old-name execution test, and retained shipped contract entry. Neither has a demonstrated final-result advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename an internal member used by a friend assembly
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agents fully implement the same minimal refactor, preserve the calculation, update the friend-assembly caller, and validate Fixture.sln successfully across both target frameworks. Their final reports differ in detail but not in substantive result quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Rename one binding without touching same-text symbols
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final results satisfy the requested surgical refactor and report equivalent successful Fixture.sln build/test validation. The difference in process detail does not indicate a difference in final code quality.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route a framework upgrade
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly follows the maintained marketplace routing evidence and gives an actionable Copilot CLI workflow while correctly limiting itself to preparation. judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are broadly correct about the conversion and the minimal Count() repair and obey the stop requirement. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route a framework upgrade
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly follows the required maintained-skill routing and gives exact Copilot CLI marketplace installation and discovery steps while preserving the project. A's central specialist identification and CLI instructions are not credible or usable, despite correctly avoiding edits and mentioning compatibility concerns.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route a test framework migration
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the stronger final response because its installation and verification guidance is actionable and host-correct, while retaining the correct specialist and mappings. Both share the notable omission of fixture-isolation risk discussion, so the overall advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route an EF Core query optimization
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills all requested preparation steps with the exact maintained skill route and actionable install, restart, and discovery instructions. A recognizes the technical issue but gives a speculative specialist and unreliable installation guidance, substantially undermining the core marketplace request.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Route runtime performance evidence
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately fulfills the requested specialist identification, vendor-neutral deployed-process framing, installation, restart, and discovery workflow while not collecting or diagnosing. A largely refuses the task and leaves every substantive requested deliverable unanswered.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Sequence distinct template and component phases
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly fulfills all requested deliverables in the required sequence with concrete Copilot CLI setup commands and does not create a project. A is an unnecessary clarification request that fails to answer the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a Python request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both violate the no-file-change requirement and otherwise remain correctly outside .NET. B is modestly stronger on the requested Python solution because its recommended indexed merge retains customer columns, unlike A's primary column-pruned implementation; however, B's single generated file improperly combines mutually alternative examples, so the advantage is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Use the Codex marketplace flow
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially more task-directed: it names the actual specialist and plugin and provides a Codex plugin workflow while avoiding a Copilot-only recommendation. Its risk explanation remains terse, but it clearly outperforms A's vague, likely unusable recommendation and commands.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully completed the refactoring task with identical, correct final results. They both: (1) renamed the implementation to `FormatReceipt`, (2) migrated the ordinary C# caller `RenderDirect`, (3) retained a private forwarding shim for reflection compatibility, (4) kept the compatibility test unchanged, and (5) verified all 17 tests pass on both .NET 8 and .NET 10. The approaches differed (Response A used sequential patches with explicit reasoning; Response B used a C# refactoring skill for guidance and applied a combined patch), but the final code quality and correctness are equivalent. No meaningful difference in outcome quality."

The only differences are operational efficiency metrics (Run 1 used fewer tokens and tool calls while Run 2 completed slightly faster in wall time), which should not be factored into quality evaluation per the rubric. The task outcome is equivalent in both cases."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create team install scripts
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B better fulfills the task requirements by providing more complete repo configuration. While both created working cross-platform scripts, Response B's key advantage is configuring global.json with both the `paths` feature (eliminating need for manual environment variable setup) and an `errorMessage` that automatically surfaces missing-SDK guidance to teammates. This makes the setup more reproducible and self-documenting. Response A's simpler approach of leaving global.json untouched and relying on README documentation is valid but less automatic and requires teammates to perform additional manual steps. Response B's configuration approach is more aligned with the task's emphasis on 'repo configuration' and enabling teammates to reproduce the setup 'on any OS after cloning' without additional manual intervention."
